column6: A vendored tokenizer vocabulary file in HuggingFace `tokenizers` JSON format (1.77 MB, one single line, zero newlines). It is a static asset under public/ that src/ts/tokenizer.ts line 314 fetches at runtime (`fetch("/token/claude/claude.json")`) and hands to @mlc-ai/web-tokenizers so the app can count tokens for Claude models. The matched text is vocabulary entries: the word pieces `"azure":13977` and, further along the same line, `"Ġrecognition":14011`, `"Face":16983`, `"Ġemotion":16789` are each just a sub-word token mapped to an integer id.
column8: The rule looks for code that infers emotion or biometric traits of a person, here keyed on an Azure Face style signal (report notes say `affect:azure_face`). At this site there is no code at all: the file is a word list the tokenizer uses to split text into token ids for counting. Tokens like `azure`, `Face`, `recognition` and `emotion` sit in the vocabulary because the base model saw those words during training, not because the app calls a face or emotion service. No camera, image or biometric input is read anywhere near this path; the file is only used to compute a token count that the UI displays. The app does have a separate 'emotion image' feature (src/ts/process/index.svelte.ts around line 2166) that asks the chat model to pick one word for a fictional character's mood from its own reply text to choose a sprite, which is text classification of the AI character's output, not inference on a person.
